1. The animation shows a grid of historical start months, running from January 1991 to July 2016. Each month is a possible date to buy a home instead of renting. A lit tile means the buyer was ahead after ten years. A dark tile means the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation labels itself "illustrative," "US only" and "history, not a forecast."

2. In frame 1, the right-hand block of tiles is dark, which means the renter came out ahead for those start months. In frames 2 to 4 those dark tiles light up and turn cream. The caption "lit again: every start 2009 to mid-2016" appears. By frames 5 and 6 nearly the whole grid is lit. The only exception is a band of brown tiles in the middle, which the legend would read as renter-ahead. The caption disappears in frame 6.

3. The grid suggests that buying beat renting over a ten-year hold for most historical start dates. Buying lost mainly in one middle stretch. The animation first shows the dark tiles for the later start dates, then lights them, so those starts also ended with the buyer ahead. I can't tell from the image alone how large the buyer's margin was. I also can't tell exactly which months make up the brown band.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer would probably take away that buying has usually paid off over a ten-year horizon in US history, with some bad start periods. The "history, not a forecast" label warns against treating that as a guarantee.

5. The picture and text suggest the pattern, but the advice is my own inference. The animation never tells viewers to buy or rent. It only says the result is historical and not a forecast.
